q: In 1678, the Dutch physicist Christiaan Huygens introduced the wave theory of light.
e: Christiaan Huygens introduced the wave theory of light in 1678.

q: In 1678, the Dutch physicist Christiaan Huygens introduced the particle theory of light.
e: Huygens introduced the wave theory of light, not the particle theory.

q: Huygens' principle states that every point on a wavefront may be considered as a source of secondary wavelets.
e: This is the exact definition of Huygens' principle.

q: Huygens' principle states that every point on a wavefront may be considered as a source of primary wavelets.
e: Every point on a wavefront is considered a source of secondary wavelets, not primary.

q: The new position of wavefront is the envelope of the wavelets.
e: The new wavefront forms the envelope of the secondary wavelets.

q: The new position of wavefront is the center of the wavelets.
e: The new position of the wavefront is the envelope, not the center, of the wavelets.

q: If the propagating wave with a frequency $f$ is transmitted through the medium at a speed $v$, then the secondary wavelets will have the same frequency and speed.
e: Secondary wavelets maintain the same frequency and speed as the propagating wave.

q: If the propagating wave with a frequency $f$ is transmitted through the medium at a speed $v$, then the secondary wavelets will have half the frequency and speed.
e: The secondary wavelets have the same frequency and speed, not half.

q: A wavefront is defined as a surface associated with a propagating wave which is a locus of all points in the wave that have the same phase.
e: This is the textbook definition of a wavefront.

q: A wavefront is defined as a surface associated with a propagating wave which is a locus of all points in the wave that have different phases.
e: A wavefront consists of points that have the same phase, not different phases.

q: Wavefront is always perpendicular to the direction of propagation or rays.
e: Wavefronts are always perpendicular to the direction of propagation.

q: Wavefront is always parallel to the direction of propagation or rays.
e: Wavefronts are always perpendicular, not parallel, to the direction of propagation.

q: There are two types of wavefront; plane wavefront and spherical wavefront.
e: The textbook identifies plane and spherical wavefronts as the two types.

q: There are three types of wavefront; plane wavefront, spherical wavefront and cylindrical wavefront.
e: The textbook explicitly states there are two types: plane and spherical wavefronts.

q: The spherical wavefront from a source transforms into plane wavefront when it is far away from the source.
e: As distance increases, the curvature decreases and it approximates a plane wavefront.

q: The plane wavefront from a source transforms into spherical wavefront when it is far away from the source.
e: It is the spherical wavefront that transforms into a plane wavefront when far away.

q: The phase angle is the position of a point on a reference circle of a waveform at an instant.
e: This matches the textbook definition of phase angle.

q: The phase angle is the position of a point on a reference line of a waveform at an instant.
e: The phase angle is measured on a reference circle, not a reference line.

q: The angular position of a point of a periodic wave is known as the phase angle.
e: Phase angle represents the angular position of a point on a periodic wave.

q: The linear position of a point of a periodic wave is known as the phase angle.
e: The phase angle is the angular position, not the linear position.

q: Path difference indicates the distance between two points measured along the direction of propagation of the wave through the medium.
e: This is the correct definition of path difference.

q: Path difference indicates the distance between two points measured perpendicular to the direction of propagation of the wave through the medium.
e: Path difference is measured along the direction of propagation, not perpendicular to it.
